newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Russian tariff seen damaging Ukraine sugar sector.
newsitem.headline: Russian tariff seen damaging Ukraine sugar sector.

text.p: Russia's decision to levy a 25 percent duty on sugar imports starting May 15 will severely hurt neighbouring Ukraine's sugar market, Western traders said on Tuesday.
"It will be tragic if they don't remove it by autumn," said one trader, adding that Ukrainian sugar would be taxed at 35 percent because of a 10 percent value added tax imposed by Russia last year.
"The chief reason for this is to maintain Russian sugar prices, which are rising, and to prevent dumping from the Ukrainian side," he said.

The trader predicted that Ukraine, which produced 3.26 million tonnes of refined sugar from its last beet crop and 3.49 million tonnes in 1995/96, would start moving whatever sugar was left over -- estimated at 300,000 tonnes -- immediately.
He also said Ukraine would continue to export to central Asian countries, which have no duties.
The Russian decree, dated April 11, excluded imports from Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, which hold customs treaties with Russia.
Another trader said the tax would hurt Ukraine's ageing refineries, since many of them barter their sugar with Russia for oil and petroleum to run their refineries.

"They already have the 10 percent duty, so that means the Ukrainian partners can provide 10 percent less. Now they will get another 25 percent less in oil and this will affect them," he said. "I'm a bit anxious about it."
The trader said that only 150 of 191 refineries were working, and only 25 of them efficiently and profitably.
Russia annually produces around two million tonnes of refined sugar, imports 1.5 million tonnes of raws for refining and imports two million tonnes of white sugar from other countries.
It has threatened since last year to restrict refined sugar imports to 1.5 million tonnes a year, including a cap on Ukraine of 1.15 million tonnes.
The second trader questioned whether Russia would maintain the duty in the long term.
"They do things, then they reconsider them," he said. "At this moment it's not that important because there isn't a lot of sugar left in Ukraine. But it's bad news anyway."

Ukraine Agriculture Minister Mykhailo Zubets, also deputy prime minister in charge of agriculture, said last week Ukraine would reduce refined sugar production because it lacked export outlets -- plans traders considered unrealistic.
